tool.name: WeightedSummaryStatistics

summary.para: Summarizes numeric attribute fields of a polyline or polygon feature class two ways, side by side: ordinary record statistics (each record one equal vote) and geometry-weighted statistics, where each record is weighted by its geodesic length (polylines) or area (polygons). For attributes that describe a per-unit-landscape property -- habitat suitability, canopy cover, resistance, road effects -- the weighted statistics are the ecologically correct description of the system. An optional case field produces one set of statistics per class; a map layer's selection is honored. No Spatial Analyst needed.

tool.usage:
Why weighted statistics are the ecologically correct description. An ordinary (unweighted) mean answers the question "what is the value of an average mapping unit?" -- every polygon casts one equal vote, so a 1-hectare sliver counts exactly as much as a 5,000-hectare wilderness block. But the animal does not live on mapping units; it lives on the land. The area-weighted mean answers the ecological question: "what is the value of an average hectare?" -- equivalently, the expected value experienced by an animal (or a random point) placed anywhere on the landscape. When a habitat model scores a large block poor and a few small patches excellent, the unweighted mean is misleadingly optimistic; the area-weighted mean tells the truth about what most of the landscape is like.
The subdivision (invariance) argument. Polygon boundaries are usually artifacts of how the data were digitized, tessellated, or unioned -- not biological entities. Split one polygon into two identical halves and nothing about the ecosystem changes, yet every unweighted statistic changes, because that polygon now casts two votes instead of one. The weighted statistics are invariant to such subdivision: however the same landscape is cut into pieces, the area-weighted mean, standard deviation, variance and median come out identical. A statistic that depends on arbitrary subdivision describes the map; a statistic that is invariant to it describes the ecological system. (This is the classic modifiable-areal-unit problem, and weighting by area is its remedy for summary statistics.)
The same logic for lines. For polylines the weight is geodesic length: the length-weighted mean of a per-kilometer attribute (traffic volume, stream gradient, fence permeability) is the true per-kilometer statistic, where the unweighted mean is an artifact of how the network happens to be split into segments.
When the unweighted statistics are the right ones. When the record is the biological unit -- one row per animal, per nest site, per discrete habitat patch whose identity matters -- each record deserves an equal vote and the ordinary statistics answer the question ("what is the mean size of a breeding patch?" is a patch-level question, not a per-hectare one). This tool always reports both families side by side, which is itself diagnostic: a large difference between MEAN and W_MEAN means the attribute is correlated with feature size (for example, high suitability concentrated in small patches), a pattern worth knowing about in its own right.
The statistics: • Unweighted (over all non-null records): count, null count, minimum, maximum, range, sum, mean, standard deviation, variance (both the n-1 sample forms), and median. • Weighted (over non-null records with positive size): total length/area used, weighted mean, weighted standard deviation, weighted variance, and weighted median.
The weighted variance uses the reliability-weights analogue of the n-1 correction -- sum(w*(x-mw)^2) / (W - sum(w^2)/W) -- which reduces exactly to the ordinary sample variance when all weights are equal, so the two families are directly comparable. The weighted median is the value at which the cumulative weight reaches half the total: half the landscape (or line length) lies at or below it.
Weights are geodesic. Lengths are geodesic meters and areas geodesic square meters, computed on the spheroid, so the statistics are correct in any coordinate system -- including geographic (latitude-longitude) data, where planar areas in squared degrees would be meaningless. Data with an unknown coordinate system falls back to planar measures in map units, with a warning.
Selections and cases. A map layer input honors its current selection, so statistics can be run on just the features of interest. The optional case field writes one row of statistics per class (per vegetation type, per ownership, per corridor alternative), like Esri's Summary Statistics case field.
Relation to other tools. Esri's Summary Statistics and the field-statistics panes compute only the unweighted family. The categorical side of the original tool -- per-class counts, proportions, lengths and areas -- lives in this add-in's Attribute Summary Reports window (Data Tools group).
Credits and references. A port of the weighted-statistics family (Mean_WBL / Mean_WBA) of the CorridorDesigner Evaluation Tools' Summary Statistics tool by Jeff Jenness. On the modifiable-areal-unit problem see: Openshaw, S. 1984. The Modifiable Areal Unit Problem. CATMOG 38. Norwich: Geo Books. https://www.uio.no/studier/emner/sv/iss/SGO9010/openshaw1983.pdf

dialogReference.para: The polyline or polygon features to summarize. A map layer's current selection is honored. Points and standalone tables are not accepted -- they have no length or area to weight by; use Esri's Summary Statistics for those.
The numeric attribute field(s) to summarize. Each field gets its own row(s) of statistics: the ordinary record statistics and the length-/area-weighted statistics side by side.

param.name: case_field
param.displayname: Case field (optional -- one row of statistics per class)

dialogReference.para: Optional grouping field (text, integer or date): one row of statistics is written per distinct value -- per vegetation type, per ownership class, per corridor alternative. Null case values group under "<Null>".

The output statistics table: one row per field (or per case value x field). A geodatabase gets a native table; a folder gets a dBASE (.dbf) table. Columns: N, N_NULL, MIN, MAX, RANGE, SUM, MEAN, STD_DEV, VARIANCE, MEDIAN, then W_TOTAL (total geodesic length/area used), W_MEAN, W_STD_DEV, W_VARIANCE and W_MEDIAN -- the weighted family. Provenance metadata is stamped on the table.

scriptExample.title: Weighted Summary Statistics example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Area-weighted habitat-suitability statistics per vegetation class.
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
arcpy.jenness.WeightedSummaryStatistics( r"C:\project\Analysis.gdb\habitat_polys", "HSI;CanopyCover", "VegClass", r"C:\project\Analysis.gdb\habitat_weighted_stats")
